questions.q: Situational awareness (situational awareness (SA)) has three levels. Level 1 is:
options: Perception — noticing the elements: train positions, alarms, weather, crowd build-up
questions.explain: Level 1 = see it. Perception gathers the raw picture before any meaning is made of it.

questions.q: Level 2 of situational awareness is:
options: Understanding what the elements mean together — e.g. late train + single spare + peak hour = headway collapse coming
Predicting the exact time of failure
questions.explain: Level 2 = understand it. Separate facts combine into one meaning — that is comprehension.

questions.q: Level 3 of situational awareness, projection, means:
options: Showing the plan on a projector
Predicting how the situation will develop in the near future and acting before it happens
questions.explain: Level 3 = predict it. The controller pre-positions the spare train BEFORE the collapse, not after.

questions.q: A controller notices a late train, knows there is only one spare, and warns stations of a coming headway collapse while pre-positioning the spare. He is demonstrating:
options: All three situational awareness (SA) levels — perception, comprehension and projection
questions.explain: See it, understand it, predict it — and act on the prediction. That is complete situational awareness.

questions.q: Situational awareness is LOST mainly by:
options: Fixation on one problem, overload, fatigue and poor handover
questions.explain: Tunnel vision, tiredness, overload and weak handovers are the classic situational awareness (SA) killers in control rooms.

questions.q: Situational awareness is PROTECTED by:
options: Structured scanning, briefings, complete shift handovers and team cross-checks
questions.explain: situational awareness (SA) survives on system habits: scanning, briefings, full handovers and colleagues who cross-check you.

questions.q: A complete shift handover must include:
options: The state of every train, defects, restrictions and pending actions — nothing 'in the head only'
questions.explain: The incoming shift inherits your picture. Anything left in your head leaves with you — and becomes their surprise.

questions.q: Degraded mode working is best described as:
options: Improvising new rules on the spot
A planned, practised way of running a reduced but safe service when part of the system has failed
Stopping all trains for any fault
questions.explain: Degraded working is a planned skill, not improvisation. Staff must be as fluent in it as in automatic running.

questions.q: Why must staff be fluent in restricted/manual procedures?
options: Because automatic running needs staff least — when automation fails, human skill carries the railway
questions.explain: Automation fails rarely but completely. The day it fails is the day manual fluency is the only thing running the service.

questions.q: Conditions change mid-shift: a section's capacity drops due to a failure. The adaptable response is:
options: Accept the lower capacity honestly, re-plan the service around it with even gaps, and inform passengers
Promise normal service to keep passengers calm
questions.explain: Adapt the plan, never the safety rules. An honest reduced service beats a fictional full one.

questions.q: During degraded working, the service promise to passengers should be:
options: A realistic reduced service — fewer trains with even gaps — honestly announced
questions.explain: Do not promise normal service on a broken railway. Even gaps and honest information keep trust and order.

questions.q: 'Protecting a usable core service rather than collapsing everything' means:
options: Running trains only near the depot
Keeping the maximum safe service running on the healthy part instead of letting the whole timetable disintegrate chasing the full plan
questions.explain: Continuity = a stable core service survives. Chasing the full timetable in degraded conditions usually collapses everything.

questions.q: Safety and service continuity are balanced by:
options: Trading a little safety for more trains
Never trading safety away, but running the maximum service possible inside the safe envelope
Stopping all service at any risk
questions.explain: Safety is the boundary, not a bargaining chip. Within it, the professional keeps the best service running.

questions.q: Weather suddenly worsens with heavy rain during the evening peak. The adaptable controller:
options: Anticipates flooding, adhesion and crowd effects, warns stations, adjusts the plan and informs passengers early
Waits for the first incident to react
questions.explain: Changing conditions demand early re-planning. Projection — acting before the effects land — is Level 3 situational awareness (SA) in action.

questions.q: A controller is fixated on one failed train while a crowd builds dangerously at another station, unnoticed. This is a failure of:
options: Situational awareness — fixation on one problem blinded him to the whole picture
questions.explain: Fixation is the textbook situational awareness (SA) loss. The whole board must keep being scanned, especially during an incident.

questions.q: Fatigue in a controller most directly damages:
options: Perception and projection — Levels 1 and 3 of situational awareness (SA)
questions.explain: Tired eyes miss indications; tired minds stop predicting. Fatigue attacks the first and last levels of situational awareness (SA).

questions.q: A junior staff member sees a developing risk that seniors have missed. Graded assertiveness requires him to:
options: Speak up clearly and immediately through the proper channel
Mention it at the next day's briefing
questions.explain: Rank never outranks a live safety observation. Speaking up is a duty, protected by procedure.

questions.q: During single-line/degraded working on one section, the rest of the line should:
options: Continue the best possible service, with the degraded section re-planned around it
Run at full speed to compensate
Be ignored by Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: One degraded section must not degrade the whole railway. Isolate the problem, serve the rest.

questions.q: Short-turning trains during a disruption is an adaptability tool because it:
options: Restores even headway on the healthy core section instead of letting gaps bunch through the failed area
questions.explain: Short turns rebuild a regular service where the railway is healthy — the core keeps its rhythm.

questions.q: When the plan must change, the change should be communicated:
options: At the end of the shift
Once, clearly, to all affected points — stations, trains and staff — so everyone works to the same new plan
questions.explain: A new plan that reaches only some points creates five different railways. One clear broadcast, all points, same plan.

questions.q: A degraded service is running with longer gaps. Passenger information should:
options: Be more frequent and honest — including expected gaps and alternatives
questions.explain: In degraded working, information is part of the service. Honest gaps and alternatives keep crowds calm and moving.

questions.q: The difference between normal and degraded working, in one line:
options: Normal = automatic running to timetable; degraded = partial failure, reduced but safely running service under adapted procedures
Degraded means staff work harder only
questions.explain: Degraded is not chaos and not closure — it is a reduced, planned, safe mode between normal and emergency.

questions.q: A new restriction is imposed on a section mid-shift. For situational awareness (SA), this restriction must be:
options: Recorded, briefed to all affected staff, and included in the shift handover
questions.explain: Restrictions live in records and handovers, not in one person's memory. That is how the next shift stays aware.

questions.q: Two trains approach a degraded section from opposite ends. The controller's situational awareness (SA) task is to:
options: Project the conflict early and regulate — hold or sequence the trains before they block each other
questions.explain: Projection exists for this moment: see the conflict before it forms and regulate while options still exist.

questions.q: Keeping one person (usually the Operations Control Centre (OCC) in-charge) free from hands-on tasks during degraded working protects:
options: The overall picture — someone must hold the whole situation while others execute tasks
questions.explain: If the in-charge dives into one task, nobody is watching the whole board. Holding the picture is itself the job.

questions.q: A driver reports worsening track conditions in rain, trip after trip. The adaptable system response is:
options: Note each report separately and forget
Recognise the trend, warn all trains, consider speed restriction per procedure and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) control for a section-level decision
Tell the driver to be careful only
Wait for an accident to confirm
questions.explain: Repeated reports are a changing condition announcing itself. Trends trigger section-level protection, not trip-level sympathy.

questions.q: Which practice best maintains situational awareness (SA) during a long, quiet night shift?
options: Relaxing scan discipline since nothing happens
Structured scanning at intervals and cross-checks, because quiet shifts breed the complacency that misses the one abnormal value
questions.explain: Quiet is an situational awareness (SA) hazard. Discipline is what carries awareness through the hours when nothing seems to happen.

questions.q: When degraded working begins, the FIRST communication priority is:
options: Ensuring every affected point knows the mode has changed and what the new plan is
questions.explain: Mode changes fail when points work to different assumptions. Tell everyone the new mode and plan, first.

questions.q: A platform screen door fault forces manual door working at one station. This is an example of:
options: A reason to close the line
Degraded working — a planned reduced procedure keeping a safe service running at that station
questions.explain: A local failure handled by a prescribed reduced procedure, service continuing safely — that is degraded working exactly.

questions.q: An adaptable operator treats an unexpected timetable change request from a station as:
options: New information to assess against the whole picture — accept, modify or refuse with reasons communicated back
questions.explain: Adaptability is not obedience or rigidity. Assess against the whole picture, decide, and communicate the decision.

questions.q: The strongest protection against situational awareness (SA) loss at shift change is:
options: A structured handover — written and verbal — covering trains, defects, restrictions, incidents and pending actions
questions.explain: Most 'new shift incidents' are old incidents whose handover was weak. Structure is the protection.

questions.q: During degraded working, promising connections and last-train commitments should be:
options: Protected where safely possible, and honestly revised where not — with passengers told early
questions.explain: Continuity includes people's onward journeys. Protect commitments where you can; where you cannot, early honesty is the service.

questions.q: A controller keeps re-checking the whole network display even while managing one degraded section. This demonstrates:
options: Maintained situational awareness beyond the immediate incident
questions.explain: The next incident rarely waits for the first to finish. Scanning the whole board during one problem is professional situational awareness (SA).

questions.q: Improvisation differs from adaptability because:
options: Adaptability works within rules and principles using practised degraded procedures; improvisation invents untested actions outside them
questions.explain: Adapt to the plan, never invent the rules. Practised degraded procedures are the adaptable operator's toolkit.

questions.q: When conditions return to normal after degraded working, the correct sequence is:
options: Resume full service instantly on one report
Confirm the failure is cleared and certified, restore in phases, inform all points, then normal working
questions.explain: Restoration is phased and certified, like the failure was managed. One optimistic report does not rebuild a timetable.

questions.q: 'Attention tunnelling' — a common cause of lost situational awareness — means:
options: Fixating on one problem or display for so long that other developing changes in the situation are missed
A type of tunnel ventilation fault
questions.explain: Under pressure, attention narrows onto the loudest problem. While the operator fights one fault, a second situation grows unseen — periodic deliberate scanning of the whole picture is the antidote.

questions.q: Conditions on a section are changing faster than the current plan can handle. The golden rule is to:
options: Keep trains moving and think faster
Return the operation to a known safe state — for example holding or stopping trains as per rules — while the new situation is assessed and a fresh plan is made
Hand the problem to the next shift
Wait for conditions to settle on their own
questions.explain: You cannot plan clearly inside a situation that is still moving. A known safe state buys the one thing decision-making needs — time — and movement can always be restarted once the picture is understood.

questions.q: 'Mode confusion' in automated systems happens when:
options: Two trains run on one line
The operator believes the system is in one automation mode while it is actually in another, and acts on the wrong belief
questions.explain: Modern systems behave differently in different modes — what the train will do 'by itself' changes. If the operator's mental picture of the mode is wrong, his correct-looking action produces a surprise. Always confirming the actual mode is a core operating habit.

questions.q: An operation is called 'resilient' mainly when it has:
options: Margins to absorb disturbance — spare trains and crew, headway margin and alternative routes — so a single failure degrades service gracefully instead of collapsing it
questions.explain: A timetable planned at 100% capacity breaks completely at the first failure. Resilience is built from deliberate slack: the spare train, the standby crew and the time margin are what adaptability spends when conditions change.

questions.q: Immediately after a sudden, unexpected event, a trained operator's first move should be a brief pause to re-orient, because:
options: There is nothing else to do
The 'startle effect' makes the first reflexive action likely to be wrong — a few seconds to perceive the real situation prevents a hasty action that worsens it
questions.explain: Startle hijacks thinking for a few seconds. Trained crews are taught to pause, look, and let perception catch up before touching controls — the pause feels slow but prevents the classic wrong first action.
